deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (§17, continued from p.177). Krafft conjectured that y_p=(2^p+1)/3 is prime whenever p is prime. He generated the values by the recursion y_{p+2}=4y_p-1. The last value, a=174763=(2^19+1)/3, was to be tested. Lexell's direct proof that it is prime begins on p.177 and finishes here.

(i) Size bound. A smallest nontrivial divisor q would satisfy q<=sqrt(174763)≈418.04, so q<419.

(ii) Residue class mod 8. Write 3a=2^19+1=2·(2^9)^2+1, a value of x^2+2y^2. Hence -2 is a quadratic residue mod q. So q≡1 or 3 (mod 8). This is end of p.177 and start of this page.

(iii) Residue class mod 38. Since q | 2^19+1, we have 2^38≡1 but 2^19≢1 (mod q). So ord_q(2)=2 or 38. Order 2 would force q=3, but 3∤174763. Hence 38 | q-1, i.e. q=19λ+1 with λ even. [Filled in by me: Euler only says λ must be even.]

(iv) Combining (ii) and (iii). Take λ mod 8:
- λ=8n gives 152n+1≡1 (mod 8): allowed.
- λ=8n+2 gives 152n+39≡7 (mod 8): excluded. The text writes this as '8n+39'.
- λ=8n+4 gives 152n+77≡5 (mod 8): excluded.
- λ=8n+6 gives 152n+115≡3 (mod 8): allowed.

So q≡1 or 115 (mod 152). The candidates listed are 1, 153, 305, 457 and 115, 267, 419. All those below 419 are composite: 153=9·17, 305=5·61, 115=5·23, 267=3·89. Hence 174763 has no prime divisor below its square root and is prime.

(v) Refutation of Krafft's conjecture. If 2p+1 is a prime ≡3 (mod 8), then 2 is a non-residue mod 2p+1. By Euler's criterion 2^p≡-1, so 2p+1 | 2^p+1. Then p=4n+1 can itself be prime. So whenever 4n+1 and 8n+3 are both prime, (2^p+1)/3 has the divisor 8n+3. Euler's examples are p=5,29,41,53,89 with divisors 11,59,83,107,179.

§18 (J. A. Euler). The solutions of x^4+1≡0 (mod p) are listed:
- p=17: x=2, 8, 9, 15
- p=41: x=3, 14, 27, 38
- p=73: x=10, 22, 51, 63
- p=89: x=12, 37, 52, 77

These are the primitive 8th roots of unity mod p. The remark that a root a yields roots a^3, a^5, a^7 is the fact that odd powers of a primitive 8th root are again primitive 8th roots.

§19. Theorem 'whose proof is wanted': if ±r is a quadratic residue mod d, then ±r is also a residue mod any prime of the form 4nr+d. In modern terms, the quadratic character of r at a prime q depends only on q mod 4r. Example: 2 is a residue mod 7 (3^2=9≡2), so 2 is a residue of every prime 8n+7. Euler's suggested 'reason' is heuristic, not a proof. It notes that a prime 8n+7 has 4n+3 nonzero square residues, whereas a composite modulus has fewer: for 15 the nonzero squares are {1,4,6,9,10}, i.e. 5 instead of 7.

§20. Theorems to be proved:
- I. If p=4n+1 is prime, then n and every divisor of n, with both signs, are quadratic residues mod p.
- II. If p=4n-1 is prime, then n and every positive divisor d of n are residues, and every -d is a non-residue.
- Generalization I': if p=4n+i^2 (i odd) is prime, then every ±d with d|n is a residue. II' (4n-i^2) continues on p.179.

Modern proof [mine]:
- For p=4n+i^2: -n≡(i/2)^2 is a square. For each odd prime q|n, p≡i^2 (mod q) and p≡1 (mod 4), so by reciprocity (q/p)=(p/q)=1. If 2|n, then p≡1 (mod 8), so (2/p)=1. Also (-1/p)=1.
- For p=4n-1 (and 4n-i^2), p≡3 (mod 4). Reciprocity gives (q/p)=(-1/q)(p/q)=(-1/q)^2=1. If 2|n, p≡7 (mod 8). And (-1/p)=-1.
errors: The first listed counterexample to Krafft's conjecture, p=5 with divisor 11, is not a counterexample: (2^5+1)/3=11 itself, which is prime. The argument needs 2p+1 to be a proper divisor; that holds for p=29,41,53,89 but not for p=5.
Notational slip: '8n+39' stands for 19(8n+2)+1=152n+39, i.e. ≡7 (mod 8). Likewise the 'forms' 8n+1, 8n+5, 8n+3 refer to the residue of 152n+c mod 8.
457 is listed among the candidates although it exceeds the bound 419. This is harmless.
The justification that λ must be even (that ord_q(2)=38, excluding q=3) is not stated on the page. It is correct but implicit.

§19: the offered 'ratio' (counting residues mod prime vs composite) is not a proof. The theorem itself is true for odd d coprime to r, which is automatic when 4nr+d is prime. It follows from quadratic (Jacobi) reciprocity.
§20: the theorems are correct but stated without proof, as Euler himself indicates ('demonstranda').

results.what: Primality proof of 174763=(2^19+1)/3 by restricting prime divisors q<sqrt N to q≡1 mod 38 and q≡1,3 mod 8 (i.e. q≡1,115 mod 152)
results.modern_name: Trial division with divisor restrictions from multiplicative order and quadratic residuosity (primality of the Wagstaff prime (2^19+1)/3)
results.usually_credited_to: Method: Fermat/Euler (divisors of a^n±1 are ≡1 mod 2n); calculation attributed here to Lexell

results.what: If 8n+3 and 4n+1 are prime then 8n+3 divides 2^(4n+1)+1; hence (2^p+1)/3 is composite for p=29,41,53,89,... refuting Krafft's conjecture
results.modern_name: Euler's criterion for (2/q); analogue of the Euler–Lagrange theorem on Mersenne numbers (2p+1 | 2^p-1 for Sophie Germain p≡3 mod 4); factors of Wagstaff numbers
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Mersenne analogue, 1750s); the Wagstaff-number analogue is folklore

results.what: Fourth roots of -1 mod 17, 41, 73, 89, and closure of the root set under odd powers
results.modern_name: Primitive 8th roots of unity mod p (p≡1 mod 8)

results.what: If ±r is a quadratic residue mod d then it is a residue mod every prime 4nr+d
results.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity (Euler's form: the character of r depends only on the prime mod 4r)

results.what: For prime p=4n+i^2 all ±d with d|n are residues; for p=4n-i^2 all +d are residues and all -d are non-residues
results.modern_name: Consequence of quadratic reciprocity; Euler's 'theorema 4ns+(2x+1)^2' formulation

deep.surprise_reason: Everything here is Euler's own known circle of ideas on residues, already published in the Opera postuma (1862). The quadratic-reciprocity formulations match his published E552. The refutation of Krafft's conjecture is a straightforward analogue of his Mersenne factor theorem. The early disproof of a 'Wagstaff prime' conjecture and Lexell's primality proof of 174763 are pleasant historical details but not major.
